title: The Prayer of Manasseh
subtitle: the worst king of Judah bends the knee of his heart
lead: The Prayer of Manasseh is a short prayer of repentance, fifteen verses long, in the voice of Manasseh, king of Judah. Kings remembers him as the worst king of all, who filled the LORD's house with altars and Jerusalem with innocent blood (2 Kings 21). Chronicles adds that the Assyrians led him to Babylon in fetters, that there "he humbled himself deeply" and prayed, and that God heard him and brought him home; the prayer, it says, was written down (2 Chronicles 33:11–19). It does not give the words. This prayer does. It praises the God who chained the sea and sealed the abyss, whose mercy has no measure (1:1–7); it says repentance was set not for the righteous but "for me, the sinner" (1:8); it confesses sins beyond the sand of the sea under the weight of a heavy iron chain (1:9–10); and it ends, "Now I bend my heart's knee" (1:11), with a plea to be let go and a vow of praise (1:12–15).

Who reads it as Scripture. The prayer has no Hebrew text and is in no book of the Hebrew Bible. Greek manuscripts copy it among the odes after the Psalms, and the Orthodox churches read it in the Great Compline, a long evening service sung mostly in Lent, and count it among their Old Testament books, though they have set no single list. The Council of Trent left it out of the Catholic canon, and the Clementine Vulgate printed it in an appendix after the New Testament. The Church of England reads it "for example of life" but not to establish doctrine, Luther kept it in his Apocrypha, and Reformed and most other Protestant churches, like Judaism, do not count it as Scripture.
facts: Read in worship and counted among the Old Testament books by the Eastern Orthodox churches (These Truths We Hold, an Orthodox Church in America catechism), which have fixed no single list. Not in the Catholic canon (Council of Trent, 1546); printed in the Clementine Vulgate's appendix. In the Apocrypha of the Church of England (Article VI), of Luther's Bible and of the KJV. Not Scripture for Reformed and most other Protestant churches, or for Judaism.
Unknown. The heading gives it to Manasseh, king of Judah (reigned fifty-five years, 2 Kings 21:1), but scholars agree it was written much later.

Debated, and not fixed by any evidence inside the prayer. Bruce Metzger: "shortly before the beginning of the Christian Era"; John Bowker: the end of the first century BC. The first known writers to use it are Christian church orders of the 200s–300s AD (the Didascalia Apostolorum and the Apostolic Constitutions), and Julius Africanus (about 221) knew the story of the prayer (Jewish Encyclopedia).
Manasseh in Assyrian captivity in Babylon, bound in chains (2 Chronicles 33:11–13), as 1:10 and 2 Chronicles 33:11 suggest.

Debated: Greek (F. C. Porter, Swete; the introduction in Charles's Apocrypha calls it "most probable"), Hebrew (Ewald; Budde, 1892), or undecided between Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek (Metzger). It survives in Greek, Latin, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopic and Old Slavonic (Metzger).

Greek: Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD), among the odes after the Psalms (Swete's base text, his Ode 8), and the Zurich Psalter (T, 600s AD), and later manuscripts; the Apostolic Constitutions (book 2, section 22). Latin: manuscripts and printed Vulgates, not Jerome's work. (Metzger's article puts the odes in "Codex B"; this page follows Swete, who prints Alexandrinus.)
A prayer of repentance in poetic Greek: praise of God (1:1–7), confession (1:8–10), plea (1:11–14), vow and doxology (1:15).
1 chapter: a heading (1:0) and 15 verses. The Plain English Translation leaves Swete's text in one place, 1:10 ("so that I cannot lift up my head"), with a variant entry.
authorship: The heading gives the prayer to Manasseh, and Christian writers from the church orders on used it as his prayer in captivity. Orthodox worship reads it without ruling on who wrote it.

A later Jewish author wrote it to supply the prayer Chronicles mentions. The Jewish Encyclopedia judged the author "evidently a Jew" of later times and said the place and date "can not be definitively" fixed; Metzger found its thought closer to Palestinian than to Greek-speaking Judaism and dated it shortly before the Christian era.
Christian origin or a Christian text?

Because its oldest known copies are in Christian works, some have asked whether Christians shaped the text. The Jewish Encyclopedia reports Eberhard Nestle's view that the text in the Greek manuscripts derives from the Apostolic Constitutions or the Didascalia, not the reverse. The introduction in Charles's Apocrypha takes the other side: it judges it "most probable that the Prayer was originally written in Greek," so that the Constitutions quote an existing prayer. Nothing in the prayer itself is distinctly Christian.

audience.to: Most likely, first, Jewish readers of Chronicles who wanted the words of the prayer it mentions (2 Chronicles 33:18–19); then Christians, whose church orders used the prayer to teach bishops to receive the repentant (the Apostolic Constitutions tell the whole story as such a lesson), and who later prayed it in worship, among the odes after the Psalms and, in the Orthodox churches, at Great Compline. If Nestle's view is right, its first readers were Christian clergy (see the views below).
audience.why: To give voice to repentance at its hardest. Manasseh was the worst king Judah had, the one Kings blames for the exile (2 Kings 24:3–4). If God heard him, no sinner is beyond hope. The prayer teaches what to say: praise God's power and mercy first, confess without excuse, ask to be let go, promise praise. Knowing the readers changes the reading: it is less a record of what one king said in Babylon than a model prayer for any sinner, which is how every church that uses it has read it.
views: Metzger and Bowker put the prayer before or around the time of Christ, among Jews who read Chronicles; the Jewish Encyclopedia judged the author a Jew.

Its oldest known setting is the Christian church orders, used to train bishops in receiving penitents. On Nestle's view, reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia, the manuscripts' text came from them; the introduction in Charles's Apocrypha holds instead that the prayer was first written in Greek and that the Constitutions quote it.

outline: God addressed: maker of all, binder of the sea and the abyss, fearsome in anger, boundless in mercy
Repentance set not for the righteous but for the sinner
Confession: sins past counting, bent by a heavy iron chain
The knee of the heart: plea to be let go and saved

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: Orthodox readers know the prayer from worship: it is read at Great Compline, sung mostly in Lent, and an Orthodox Church in America parish's catechism says the church "accepts these books as being canonical" while not using them as primary sources for dogma. The lens reads it as the church's own prayer of repentance.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Scholars read it as an anonymous prayer written to fill the gap of 2 Chronicles 33:18–19, debating its original language (Greek or Hebrew), its date (most put it before or around the time of Christ) and whether its first known home, in Christian church orders, says anything about where it came from.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: The prayer is not in the Jewish Bible, and the Jewish Encyclopedia found no trace of it in Jewish tradition; but the rabbis argued over whether Manasseh's repentance was accepted (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and later legends told how he prayed. The lens sets the prayer beside them.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who study the world of the first Christians: penitence and God's mercy toward sinners as the Gospels voice them (repentance for sinners, not the righteous, Luke 5:32; "me, the sinner," Luke 18:13). The links are echoes of shared Jewish speech, not quotations.

lenses.name: Western churches: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic and Protestant readers: the Council of Trent left it out and the Clementine Vulgate put it in an appendix; the Church of England reads it "for example of life" but not for doctrine; Luther kept it among the Apocrypha; Reformed churches do not count it as Scripture.

sections.h: How to read the Prayer of Manasseh
sections.b: Read it with 2 Chronicles 33 open. The prayer names no city and no Assyrian king, but every line has its place in Chronicles: the fetters (2 Chronicles 33:11) and the iron chain (1:10), the humbling (2 Chronicles 33:12; 1:10–11), the idols (2 Chronicles 33:3–7; 1:10), the God who hears (2 Chronicles 33:13; 1:13–14). Then read it as a prayer, out loud: it is built to be prayed, with doubled pleas ("I have sinned, Lord, I have sinned"; "let me go free, Lord, let me go free") and a close of praise.

In Greek manuscripts of the Psalter, a set of "odes" or canticles follows the Psalms: songs and prayers from elsewhere in the Bible, such as the songs of Moses and Hannah and the prayers of Jonah and Habakkuk, collected for worship. Codex Alexandrinus includes the Prayer of Manasseh among them, and Swete prints it as the eighth; the Zurich Psalter counts it as the ninth. The Orthodox Psalter in use today has nine Odes, without this prayer (Asser's Psalter of 2005, after the Athens edition of 1985), and the prayer is read instead in Great Compline.

Kings and Chronicles agree on Manasseh's sins and disagree on his end. Kings has no repentance and lays the exile at his door (2 Kings 21:10–16; 2 Kings 24:3–4). Chronicles tells of his capture, prayer, return and reforms (2 Chronicles 33:10–16). Chronicles names its own sources for the prayer, "the records of the kings of Israel" and "the records of Hozai" (2 Chronicles 33:18–19). The prayer takes Chronicles' side and makes the most of it.

The Plain English Translation is made from the Greek of Swete's Old Testament in Greek, which prints Codex Alexandrinus, compared with Brenton's English (1851) and the KJV Apocrypha. It departs from Swete once, at 1:10, where Alexandrinus reads "for me to throw my head back over my sins" and the Zurich Psalter's "so that I cannot lift up my head" is followed (see the variant); Swete's and Rahlfs's printed texts both keep Alexandrinus's wording, so this is the writer's judgment, not an editor's choice. Brenton and the KJV Apocrypha have a longer text in several places, above all two extra lines at the end of 1:7, which the Apostolic Constitutions and the Latin also have; each is given as a variant. The verse is set out in lines like a psalm.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the chained king and the chained sea
spec.body: The prayer opens with God "putting the sea in fetters" and sealing the abyss (1:3) and comes to the king bent by a heavy iron chain (1:10) and begging "let me go free" (1:13). Claude suggests the writer built the prayer on that contrast: the God who binds even chaos can loose a chained man. The plea of 1:13 asks God to do for Manasseh the opposite of what he does to the sea. No source opened for this page says this.

In a dark stone cell in Babylon, a Judean king with a broken crown on the floor beside him kneels bent nearly double under a heavy iron chain on his neck and wrists; his face is turned down, eyes closed, lips moving in prayer; a thin shaft of light falls from a high slit window onto him; on the wall behind, faint shapes of the idols and star-symbols he once worshiped fade into shadow.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. traditions.q: Where does the Prayer of Manasseh sit: Scripture, a book read in church, or neither?
views: Read in worship at Great Compline, mostly in Lent, as the third psalm of the service's second part (DiPippo). These Truths We Hold, published by St. Tikhon's Seminary Press and given by an Orthodox Church in America parish, lists it among the books outside the Hebrew canon, which the church "accepts ... as being canonical" and "uses ... liturgically" but does not use as primary sources for dogma.

Not Scripture. The Council of Trent's list (1546) does not include it. The Clementine Vulgate placed it after the New Testament with 3 and 4 Esdras, outside "the series of canonical Scripture," saying the prayer is part of no canonical book.

Read, not for doctrine. Article VI lists "The Prayer of Manasses" among the other books which "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine."
Kept among the Apocrypha. The Jewish Encyclopedia notes that Luther retained it, and Metzger that Luther's Bible put it at the close of the Apocrypha.
Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the books commonly called Apocrypha, "not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of Scripture."

canon.summary: The Prayer of Manasseh is read in Orthodox worship and counted among the Old Testament books by the Orthodox churches, which have fixed no single list. The Catholic Church left it out at Trent and printed it in an appendix; the Church of England and Luther keep it among the Apocrypha, read but not for doctrine; Reformed and most other Protestant churches and Judaism do not count it as Scripture.
accepted_by: Read in worship: the prayer is the third psalm of the second part of Great Compline, the long evening service sung mostly in Lent (DiPippo). These Truths We Hold (St. Tikhon's Seminary Press, 1986), as given by an Orthodox Church in America parish, calls it "read at the Great Compline Service" and counts it among the books the Orthodox Church "accepts ... as being canonical," but does not use "as primary sources in the definition of her dogmas." This is the Eastern Orthodox use. Metzger lists Armenian, Ethiopic and Syriac manuscripts of the prayer.

Not Scripture. The Council of Trent (1546) did not include it. The Clementine Vulgate printed it after the New Testament with 3 and 4 Esdras, outside "the series of canonical Scripture." Before Trent, printed Vulgates had placed it after 2 Chronicles (Metzger).
Church of England and the Anglican Communion
A book read, not for doctrine: Article VI names "The Prayer of Manasses" among the books read "for example of life and instruction of manners." It is in the Apocrypha of the KJV.
Kept in the Apocrypha of Luther's Bible, at its close (Jewish Encyclopedia; Metzger).
Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says the Apocrypha "are no part of the Canon of Scripture."
Not Scripture. It is not in the Hebrew Bible, and the Jewish Encyclopedia found "no trace" of the prayer in Jewish tradition, though the rabbis debated Manasseh's repentance (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2).

provenance.h: A prayer to fill a gap
provenance.b: Chronicles twice says Manasseh's prayer was written down, in "the records of the kings of Israel" and "the records of Hozai" (2 Chronicles 33:18–19), but gives no words. The Prayer of Manasseh supplies them. It is not that lost record: it has no Hebrew text, it names nothing from the story but its iron chain and idols, and its first known readers are much later.

The oldest known writings to contain it are Christian church orders. The Jewish Encyclopedia says the Didascalia gives it after a mention of 2 Chronicles 33, and the Apostolic Constitutions (book 2, section 22) give the whole story of Manasseh, his chains, his prayer in full and a flame of fire that made the shackles fall off, as a lesson for bishops on repentance. The same article reports that Julius Africanus (about 221) knew the story that Manasseh's bonds burst while he was reciting a hymn. Among Bible manuscripts, Codex Alexandrinus (400s AD) has it among the odes after the Psalms.

The Greek is formal and careful. F. C. Porter and Swete held that it was composed in Greek, and the introduction in Charles's Apocrypha calls this "most probable"; Ewald and Karl Budde (1892) argued for a Hebrew original (Jewish Encyclopedia). Metzger called the question disputed between Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, and dated the prayer "shortly before the beginning of the Christian Era"; Bowker gives the end of the first century BC. Nothing in the prayer fixes a date.

provenance.h: A different Manasseh prayer at Qumran
provenance.b: Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the collection of psalms numbered 4Q381 contains a Hebrew prayer connected with Manasseh, a separate composition from this one. Mika Pajunen's 2012 article studies it beside 2 Chronicles 33 (only its bibliographic record was opened for this page).

rejected_why.b: Judaism and the churches that follow the Hebrew canon (Reformed and most other Protestants) count only books of the Hebrew Bible as the Old Testament. This prayer has no Hebrew text at all.

The Council of Trent's list leaves it out. The preface of the Clementine Vulgate gave the reasons for printing it outside the canonical books: it "exists neither in Hebrew nor even in Greek," is not found in the older manuscripts, and is part of no canonical book. The first reason was mistaken, since the prayer survives in Greek, but the others express the main point: no church council or ancient list had counted it as a book.

rejected_why.h: Read for life, not for doctrine
rejected_why.b: The Church of England's Article VI and Luther's Bible kept it among books useful to read but not to settle doctrine. The Westminster Confession went further: the Apocrypha "are no part of the Canon of Scripture" and are to be used like other human writings.

cited_in.b: Chronicles tells that Manasseh prayed in captivity and was heard, and says the prayer was written down (2 Chronicles 33:18–19). The prayer claims to be that prayer. No book of the 66 quotes it.

The tax collector's "me, the sinner" uses the same Greek words as 1:8, and both speak of not raising the eyes to heaven (1:9). This is shared speech about repentance; there is no evidence Luke knew the prayer.
"I have come to call sinners to repentance," not the righteous; compare Luke 15:7. The same contrast as 1:8, in the same Greek words, but no sign of borrowing either way.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to how Jews and early Christians prayed about repentance, the prayer is valuable and clear. As a text, it survives in Greek in a few manuscripts and church orders that differ in small ways, with one hard place (1:10). As history, it is not Manasseh's own prayer in any provable sense: it has no Hebrew text and no known reader before the Christian church orders. As teaching, it agrees closely with the Bible's own words about God's mercy and repentance, with one exaggeration (the sinless patriarchs, 1:8).

sections.b: The prayer gathers the Bible's language of mercy (Exodus 34:6; Joel 2:13; Psalm 51) into a model confession. Its stress on God as "the God of those who repent" fits Jewish piety of the last centuries before Christ (Jewish Encyclopedia; Metzger) and the preaching of repentance in the Gospels.

Swete's notes show the Zurich Psalter differing from Codex Alexandrinus in many small places, and the English of Brenton and the KJV Apocrypha follows a longer form with two extra lines at 1:7, which the Apostolic Constitutions and the Latin also have. None of these changes the prayer's meaning, except the hard line of 1:10, where the Plain English Translation follows the Zurich Psalter against the printed texts of Swete and Rahlfs (a judgment explained in the variant).

sections.h: Its claim to be Manasseh's prayer
sections.b: The heading is a literary frame. Scholars agree the prayer was written centuries after Manasseh. Orthodox worship reads it without deciding the question; for those who pray it, the point is that the words fit any sinner as they would have fit him.

It agrees with the Bible on God's power over creation (Job 38:8–11), his anger at sin and greater mercy (Exodus 34:6–7), and salvation by mercy, not merit (Psalm 51:1). It goes beyond Genesis in calling the patriarchs sinless (1:8; compare Genesis 12:11–13; Genesis 27:18–24). It does not conflict with Chronicles; it gives the words Chronicles leaves out. Churches that use it in worship read it in this way, as a prayer that teaches what the Bible teaches.

how_to_read.b: Read 2 Chronicles 33:1–20 first, then the prayer. It is a window into a moment the Bible describes but does not show.
Its shape, praise, confession, plea, vow, is a pattern for prayer. Read it aloud, slowly, the way the Orthodox read it at Great Compline, mostly in Lent.
Where it says what the Bible says, it is a faithful echo. Where it goes further (the patriarchs "had not sinned"), read it as a way of speaking, not as teaching.
